_note: DECLARED / INDUCED learning outcomes for the book. Each outcome has a PRIMARY unit (where it is chiefly taught — drives coverage) and optional secondary_units (elaborative: reinforce/extend/apply). Keys are outline unit ids (section_id | chapter-slug | part-N | book). Hand-authored SOURCE — this file IS edited by hand; outcomes.json + outcomes-draft.md are generated from it. Each declaration: {granularity (of the primary), primary_unit, secondary_units?, verb (from BLOOM_VERBS), obj, statement?, provenance, anchor?, gap_note?}. provenance is 'derived' (grounded in what the primary unit actually teaches — cite the grounding prose in anchor), 'declared' (thin prose roughly supports it), or 'gap-recommended' (content the unit ought to deliver but does not yet — cite gap_note). COVERAGE: primary drives it; an elaborative-only unit is still a gap. Do NOT manufacture aspirational outcomes to fill slots. See book-models/DESIGN.md 2.6.

declarations.obj: one-shot scripting from supervised autonomy
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can distinguish one-shot scripting from supervised autonomy and name what each supplies to the agent.

declarations.obj: how long a leash a task can run on from the model's data density and capability
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can judge how long a leash a task can run on from two factors — how densely the model's training data covers the work and how capable the model is at it — and see why misjudging the mode is costly either way.

declarations.obj: why an agent needs a model of how to build the thing, not just a picture of it
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can explain why an agent, like a 3D printer, needs the detailed build instructions and not merely a picture of the desired result.

declarations.obj: the posture that when an agent produces the wrong thing, the first suspect is the instructions
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can adopt the posture that an agent is a printer, not a stapler — so when it produces the wrong thing, the first suspect is the instructions, and the models can build anything one can explain.

declarations.obj: agent work as a fixed-shape loop engineered around a measurable metric
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can describe agent work as a fixed-shape loop — input, reasoning, output, fed around again — and see why engineering it starts with a measurable success metric.

declarations.obj: how a model of the world conditions the agent's search toward the answer
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can explain why handing the agent a model of its world conditions the probability distribution of its behavior — aiming its search and shrinking what it must hold.
declarations.anchor: point: model-of-the-world-is-the-input-agent-reasons-over / structuring-loop-and-model-conditions-the-distribution (section opens on an aside, not a topic sentence — the O2 gap the drain records)

declarations.obj: a governed environment in which a fleet of coding agents does useful engineering work at bounded risk
declarations.statement: After the book, the reader can design a governed engineering environment in which a fleet of coding agents produces correct work at bounded risk — choosing the right mechanism, the right model, and the right transformation for each failure class.
declarations.anchor: Preface 'mechanize discipline' + the book's stated aim (SE-at-Google + GoF touchstones): patterns that keep a fleet productive at bounded failure.

declarations.obj: a constraint from a sensor and a soft mechanism from a hard one
declarations.statement: After the book, the reader can situate any governance move on the two thesis axes — constraint-vs-sensor and soft-vs-hard — and reach for the one the failure calls for.
declarations.anchor: The two book-thesis axes (Alignment: constraint/sensor; soft/hard) run through Part 2 (constraints-and-sensors) and Part 4 (from-soft-to-hard, in the governance-conversion chapter).

declarations.obj: a system as a small set of structured, drift-checked 4+1 views
declarations.statement: After the book, the reader can model a system as structured, drift-checked views an agent reasons through, rather than leaving the structure in a human's head.
declarations.anchor: The Modeling Thesis, developed across Part 3 (the executable 4+1 zoo).

declarations.obj: whether a task needs the book's machinery at all, and read an agent as a loop that needs a model
declarations.statement: After Part 1, the reader can judge which tasks warrant governance machinery and which do not, and read an agent as a loop that needs a model of its world.
declarations.anchor: 1.1 'Not every programming task needs the machinery this book describes' + 1.3 'an agent runs in a loop … give it a model of the world'.

declarations.obj: the governed environment — its layers, its ex-ante and ex-post mechanisms, its lifecycles, and its metrics
declarations.statement: After Part 2, the reader can construct a governed engineering environment: place a control at the right layer of the agent stack, split ex-ante from ex-post, write lifecycles and runbooks, and measure one level deeper.
declarations.anchor: Part 2 chapter arc: agent-stack -> semantic-gap -> ex-ante/ex-post -> lifecycles/runbooks -> metrics -> guardrails-collide.

declarations.obj: a system through Kruchten's 4+1 views as structured models an agent reasons through
declarations.statement: After Part 3, the reader can model a system as the executable 4+1 zoo — logical, process, development, physical, and scenario views — each a structured model kept honest by a drift check.
declarations.anchor: Part 3 is the 4+1 views one chapter each (3.2 logical, 3.3 process, 3.4 development, 3.5 physical, 3.6 scenarios), spined by 3.1.

declarations.obj: the method to a real codebase — running the MAGE workflow loop, inducing models from brownfield code, wielding the skills, holding the result with generative validation, and converting recurring failures into mechanisms
declarations.statement: After Part 4, the reader can put the method to work: run the MAGE workflow loop, induce models from an existing codebase, deploy the self-operate / self-govern / self-communicate skills, hold the result with generative validation, and convert a recurring failure into a durable mechanism.
declarations.anchor: Part 4 title 'Putting It to Work' + chapter arc: the-mage-workflow -> brownfield -> skills -> generative-validation -> governance-conversion -> field-guide.

declarations.obj: the method's evolution through a real accessibility-remediation system
declarations.statement: After Part 5, the reader can trace how the method grew from a single reviewer to a multi-agent engineering organization in one real system, and relate each governance move to the problem that forced it.
declarations.anchor: Part 5 is the ADA/DocAble case study: context -> timeline/work -> built-system -> road-to-MAGE (role progression).

declarations.obj: what the method changes for how software engineering is measured, staffed, and taught
declarations.statement: After Part 6, the reader can evaluate the method's implications for the discipline — where the judgment moved, what stays human, and where models become the universal language of engineering.

declarations.obj: when an open-ended task needs governance and who is accountable when an agent gets it wrong
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can judge whether a task is open-ended enough to need the book's machinery, and reason about accountability when an agent produces a wrong result.
declarations.anchor: Section titles: 'What this book is about (and what it is not)', 'an-open-ended-technology', 'whose-fault-is-it'.

declarations.obj: the system the book's claims are grounded in — what it does, how its six parts fit, why it was built — and the governance-conversion move on two real incidents
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can describe the grounding case — what DocAble does, how its six parts fit together, and why it was built — and recognize the convert-a-failure-into-a-mechanism move in its first two incidents.

declarations.obj: why an agent is a loop and why it needs a model of its world
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can explain the agent as a fixed-shape loop and why giving it a model of the world is the first act of governance.
declarations.anchor: Section titles 'everything-is-a-loop' + 'give-it-a-model-of-the-world'; ts: 'an agent runs in a loop, and the loop has a fixed shape'.

declarations.obj: the two theses and the governed engineering environment from the substrate's properties — four of the foundation model, four of the harness
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can derive the Modeling and Alignment theses from the properties of the foundation model and the agentic harness, and say why their combination requires the governed engineering environment.

declarations.obj: the four layers of the agent stack as four places to steer
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can identify the four layers of the agent stack and read each as a distinct place to insert a control.

declarations.obj: the four layers of the agent stack — foundation model, harness, engineering environment, application — and the grip each gives
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can identify each of the four layers of the agent stack, from the foundation model up, and name the kind of governance grip each one gives.

declarations.obj: why every layer of the stack is an injection opportunity serving the one goal of narrowing the agent's search
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can explain why each layer of the stack is an injection opportunity, all serving one goal — narrowing the agent's search — and why the mechanisms placed there must themselves be governed for interplay.

declarations.obj: why a structured model sits at the apex of the documentation hierarchy and what a drift check does and does not prove
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can explain why a structured model beats prose and code as the thing an agent reasons through, and why a drift check proves agreement, not correctness.

declarations.obj: words (too soft) from code (too verbose) and place a model as the compact, unambiguous sweet spot between them
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can distinguish soft prose from verbose code and explain why a model — accurate, unambiguous, yet compact — is the sweet spot an agent can reason over.

declarations.obj: why hand-maintained models rotted and why an agent fleet flips the calculation
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can explain why hand-maintained models drifted and fell out of favor, and why agents — which reason over models, not code — flip that calculation when a linked set of models is kept in sync.

declarations.obj: why a structured model at the apex of the documentation hierarchy binds docs, code, and tests into a checkable whole
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can explain why the apex of the documentation hierarchy is a structured model — the one description a machine can read and check the others against, binding docs, code, and tests where structured English stops one rung short.

declarations.obj: the modeling choice on a spectrum from no modeling to an executable model, an economic call whose sweet spot agents move outward
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can situate how far to model on a spectrum trading strength against changeability, and read the choice as an economic call whose sweet spot agents have moved outward.

declarations.obj: the semantic-gap fix to the operator's own loop — a bank-hook checking fullness and staleness together
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can apply the semantic-gap fix to a second, operator-loop instance: a hook that fires on context-fullness and record-staleness together, and can name why even a roughly-right rung beats a hook that sits too late.

declarations.obj: ex-ante from ex-post decisions and a constraint from a sensor
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can split what is decidable up front from what is learned by building, and classify each mechanism as a constraint (prevent) or a sensor (catch).

declarations.obj: specification-driven development to what you know up front — write the rule, then determinize it with a cheap agent-written check
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can apply specification-driven development to what is knowable up front: write every known rule down and determinize it with a cheap deterministic check the agent itself writes.

declarations.obj: why most real mechanisms are built ex-post, from failures no specification predicted
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can explain why governance is built ex-post — iteratively, as unforeseen failures reveal themselves — and why that is where most real mechanisms come from rather than a fallback for a weak plan.

declarations.obj: a lifecycle and a runbook that splits the deterministic from the judgment
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can author a lifecycle and its runbook, giving the deterministic parts a tight algorithm and the judgment parts the roughest one that still fits.

declarations.obj: a metric that measures one level deeper than the surface number
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can design a metric that measures one level deeper — turning a number that reports into one that drives a decision — and place it on the hard-to-soft spectrum, feeding a hard number into a structured model the metric tool then consumes.

declarations.obj: what lies between controls when guardrails collide, using a governance graph
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can analyze the space between controls with a governance graph — nodes tagged by event and resource, edges a closed conflict taxonomy joined by the shared resource — and reason about mechanisms whose hooks they do not own.

declarations.obj: the collisions between controls as edges in a governance graph joined by the shared resource
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can analyze the space between controls with a governance graph — mechanisms as nodes tagged by event and resource, conflicts as edges in a closed contradiction/contention/ordering/precedence taxonomy joined by the shared resource — and route each edge to a lint or a human prompt by its type before the control ships.

declarations.obj: the governance graph to hooks you did not author, checking a merged graph for unresolved contradiction
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can apply the governance graph to hooks they did not author — entering an outside hook as a node on a conservative possible-conflict edge against its whole slot until analyzed — and reduce satisfying one or several regulators to checking that the merged graph carries no unresolved contradiction, including that no required hard block is overridden by a soft aim.

declarations.obj: the two disciplines that keep a governance graph honest — symbol-anchoring and a descriptive, not aspirational, model
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can justify the two disciplines that keep a governance graph honest — anchoring each node to its control's code by symbol so a drift lint reddens an unmodeled control, and keeping the model descriptive rather than inventing conflict-lints for collisions that never happened.

declarations.obj: why a fleet pays for free the modeling expense that once buried MBSE
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can explain why the cost that sank classical MBSE is one an agent fleet absorbs, and read Kruchten's 4+1 as the spine of the model zoo.

declarations.obj: a service-flow model and the domain registries it rests on
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can model the logical view as a structured service-flow model backed by frozen domain registries.
declarations.anchor: Section titles 'service-flow-model' + 'domain-registries'; ts: 'The typed source-of-truth for a service-oriented architecture'.

declarations.obj: the concurrency of a system with a synchronization model and formal invariant verification
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can model the process view — cataloging every lock in a synchronization model and backing its invariants with formal verification.
declarations.anchor: Section titles 'formal-invariant-verification' + 'synchronization-model' (ts: 'A typed registry that models the system's synchronization behavior — every OS-level lock').

declarations.obj: a codebase's zones with a component & zone model and a rule-metadata registry
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can model the development view — every component's zone and the governance rules that ride it — as typed registries.
declarations.anchor: Section titles 'component-zone-model' + 'rule-metadata-registry'; ts: 'A typed catalog of every component's code zone'.

declarations.obj: where a system runs with a deployment-topology model and an invariant-DAG execution policy
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can model the physical view — deployment topology and a typed deploy DAG — and name the one honest gap in the cost view.

declarations.obj: user and developer journeys to test placement through a chain of structured models
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can map journeys to the environment tier that tests them, joining user-journey, orchestration, criticality, and coverage models.

declarations.obj: three approaches to inducing a model from existing code
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can apply top-down, bottom-up, and lint-cover-then-induce approaches to bring a brownfield codebase under a model.

declarations.obj: the self-operate, self-governance, and self-communicate skills, and the recipe for minting new ones
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can use the three packaged skills and follow the construction recipe to mint a new one well.

declarations.obj: a transformation to the model it produces and the guarantee it must carry
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can size a transformation to its model and guarantee, and tell a right-sized leap from a wrong-shaped one.

declarations.obj: where a model's training-data bias helps and where MBSE earns its keep on the novelty axis
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can analyze how training-data bias shapes an agent's reach, and situate MBSE on the novelty axis where it shines.

declarations.obj: the agent-shaped failure modes and the disciplines that survive them
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can recognize the recurring agent-shaped failure modes — optionality, false 'done', broken estimates, vibe coding — and adopt the disciplines that survive them.
declarations.anchor: The quotable-lessons strip (each failure mode paired with the discipline it demands) plus the failure incidents 'The decision left open', '"Done" was a claim', and 'Lessons that recur without a single scene' in the merged 5.6 conversions chapter (identity label 'failures').

declarations.obj: among property testing, fuzzing, and fuzz-MBSE by which specification a generator hunts against
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can choose among generative-validation strategies by the specification each one attacks, treating the structured model as an oracle.

declarations.obj: why document accessibility is a hard, high-burden problem worth this machinery
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can explain the accessibility problem the case-study system solves and why a document is not just a file.

declarations.obj: the stages, velocity, and kinds of work the case-study system required
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can describe how the case-study project unfolded across its stages and the range of work it demanded.

declarations.obj: the built system through three views of the same architecture
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can analyze the built system end-to-end through three complementary views over one shared edit language.

declarations.obj: the author's path from solo co-coder to tech lead of an agent crew
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can trace the role progression — co-coder, QA, review-lead, tech-lead — that grew a single developer into an agent organization.

declarations.obj: what the method changes for how software engineering is measured, staffed, and taught
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can evaluate the discipline-level implications: where judgment moved, what saturates, and why models are the universal language of engineering.

declarations.obj: the part of the engineering work that stays the reader's own, and where to take the method next
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can identify the part of the work that stays human and choose where to go next.

declarations.obj: the book within the software-engineering literature — Software Engineering at Google, the Gang of Four, and Model-Driven Software Engineering
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can situate MAGE within the software-engineering literature — mechanized discipline (SE at Google), the design-pattern form (the Gang of Four), and the modeling tradition (MDSE) — as older aspirations under new economics.
declarations.anchor: Section titles 'the-same-two-questions-four-answers', 'standing-on-three-books' (Software Engineering at Google, the Gang of Four, Model-Driven Software Engineering), 'older-aspirations-new-economics', 'placing-mage'.

declarations.obj: six independent industrial systems as evidence for and against MAGE's claims — the modeling ceiling, the convergence buckets, and the governance census — without mistaking corroboration for a controlled test
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can analyze six independent industrial systems as evidence for and against MAGE's claims — the modeling ceiling where the software-first sites fall silent, the convergence buckets they share anyway, and the governance census that turns description into diagnosis — without mistaking corroboration across reconstructions for a controlled test.

declarations.obj: why studying a governed environment demands a new empirical regime — fallible oracles, the limits of per-task ablation, deep single-case evidence, and a fixed intelligence input
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can evaluate why a governed environment demands a new empirical regime: the oracle is itself fallible, per-task ablation cannot price the environment, deep single-case evidence is a legitimate method, and the intelligence input must be held fixed to measure what the environment does.

declarations.obj: the MAGE theory as a causal-loop dynamic model — its constructs, feedback dynamics, hypotheses, propositions, and predictions
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can explain the MAGE theory as a causal-loop dynamic model: its constructs, the four feedback dynamics, the seven hypotheses and two propositions, and the predictions and research agenda they imply.

declarations.obj: a constraint from a sensor — prevent the mistake versus catch it — and place both on the independent soft-versus-hard form axis
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can distinguish a constraint (prevent, costs no iteration) from a sensor (catch, costs iterations), place both on the independent soft-versus-hard axis, and tag most real mechanisms as a package by their primary move.

declarations.obj: a metric one level deeper than the number a decision needs
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can apply Ousterhout's rule and measure one level deeper than the surface number — reading a per-service cost split or a boot-time breakdown as a decision the invoice-level number buried.

declarations.obj: a hard, machine-read metric whose defining move is that the number feeds a structured model
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can analyze a hard, deterministic metric at the level where the decision lives — reading cold-start latency one level deeper to name runtime initialization rather than scale-from-zero, computing a longest-path worst case over a service graph, and feeding the number into a structured deployment model a recompute tool consumes.

declarations.obj: coverage measured one level deeper — model-claim coverage joined from a traceability graph and the coverage oracle
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can compute coverage measured one level deeper — joining a traceability graph's claim-to-anchor edges with the coverage oracle so the metric counts model claims instead of lines, names an unexercised invariant instead of a percentage, and reports an honest exercised/unmeasurable/out-of-surface breakdown.

declarations.obj: a soft, judgment-laden metric that aims a reader and must not be wired to a gate
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can classify a soft metric — a doc-derived test's coverage-of-doc-claims — as one that aims a reader rather than deciding, recognize why its softness is inseparable from a readiness judgment about the seam, and see why wiring it to a blocking gate manufactures hollow tests.

declarations.obj: why a structured model is not a picture of the metric machinery but the machinery itself
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can explain why the MBSE models are consumed at runtime to produce the metrics — the cold-start numbers and the coverage graph both read at check time — so a component-distance grade read from the model drives a pre-commit gate three ways, the model being the machinery rather than a picture of it.

declarations.obj: why a drift check proves agreement between model and code, not correctness of either
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can explain the precise guarantee a drift check gives — agreement, not correctness — and why only a model authored from intent, not derived from code, catches a wrong "is".

declarations.obj: the semantic gap between a model and the code it governs
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can define the semantic gap — enforcing a property at the wrong level of abstraction — and identify the level where it becomes legible.

declarations.obj: a mechanism on the soft-to-hard spectrum by whether it aims or holds

declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can identify each of the four layers of the agent stack.

declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can author a runbook that separates deterministic steps from judgment ones — giving the deterministic parts an executable tool that also yields a reusable trace, and the judgment parts a rubric or the roughest algorithm that still fits, up to a pre-canned brief for delegation.

declarations.obj: a lifecycle's healthy path and the failure states off each node, naming the way out and the prohibition
